raw_case_text:
A 43-year-old man, a resident of Uttar Pradesh, driver by occupation, a smoker for 25 years, and occasional alcohol consumer, having a previous history of dengue fever six years back, known patient of diabetes mellitus, presented with a history of acute onset intermittent, high-grade fever associated with chills during the last seven days followed by mild to moderate epigastric pain and two episodes of gum bleeding. He also noticed yellowish discoloration of eyes for three to four days, and throat pain for two days. On examination, the patient was hemodynamically stable with a random blood sugar of 180 mg/dL and had multiple ecchymoses over the arm and abdomen, icterus, and multiple creamy white patches over the tongue, posterior oro-pharyngeal wall and palate (Figures 2A, 2B). Tenderness was noted on the right hypochondriac region; on respiratory system examination, the patient had inspiratory crackles over bilateral infra-axillary and infra-scapular areas. The rest of the systemic examination was unremarkable.
Baseline blood investigation showed hematocrit of 39.7%, thrombocytopenia of 19,000/mm3, and total leukocyte count of 6,700/mm3; liver function test showed total bilirubin of 3.56 mg/dL, direct bilirubin of 2.00 mg/dL, SGPT of 450 Units/liter and SGOT of 633 Units/liter, with alkaline phosphatase of 559 Units/liter. The renal function test was within normal limits. A tropical fever workup came positive for dengue NS1 (ELISA method), and viral markers (anti-HCV, anti-HIV I/II, and HBsAg) were non-reactive. Serum HBA1C level was 10%. Fundoscopy showed no evidence of hypertensive or diabetic retinopathy, and urine routine microscopy showed no evidence of proteinuria. Abdominal ultrasonography showed grade II fatty liver with coarse liver echotexture without any sign of portal hypertension or dilatation of biliary radicle. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed evidence of oro-pharyngeal candidiasis but not esophageal involvement or any varices there.
The patient improved with conservative management and transfusion of random donor platelets. Oral thrush improved with nystatin suspension, 4 mL four times a day. Over the next two weeks, the patient reported a complete resolution of throat pain. Blood glucose was optimized using subcutaneous regular insulin (10U three times a day) in the outpatient setting.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 43-year-old male driver from Uttar Pradesh presented with intermittent high-grade fever and chills for 7 days, followed by epigastric pain, gum bleeding, jaundice for 3-4 days, and throat pain for 2 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed acute-onset intermittent high-grade fever with chills 7 days prior to admission, followed by mild-to-moderate epigastric pain, two episodes of gingival bleeding, yellowish discoloration of the eyes for 3-4 days, and throat pain for 2 days.
subjective.past_medical_history: Known diabetes mellitus; history of prior dengue fever 6 years earlier; 25-year smoking history and occasional alcohol consumption.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high-grade fever, chills, epigastric pain, gum bleeding (2 episodes), scleral icterus, and throat pain.

objective.physical_examination: Hemodynamically stable; icterus, multiple ecchymoses over the arms and abdomen, and multiple creamy white patches over the tongue, posterior oropharyngeal wall, and palate. Respiratory exam showed bilateral infra-axillary and infrascapular inspiratory crackles; abdominal exam showed right hypochondriac tenderness. Fundoscopy was negative for diabetic or hypertensive retinopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Random blood sugar 180 mg/dL, serum HbA1c 10%, hematocrit 39.7%, platelet count 19,000/mm3, total leukocyte count 6,700/mm3, total bilirubin 3.56 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.00 mg/dL, SGPT (ALT) 450 U/L, SGOT (AST) 633 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 559 U/L, normal renal function tests, normal urinalysis without proteinuria, and non-reactive anti-HCV, anti-HIV I/II, and HBsAg. Abdominal ultrasound showed grade II fatty liver with coarse echotexture without portal hypertension or biliary dilatation. Upper GI endoscopy confirmed oropharyngeal candidiasis without esophageal involvement or varices.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Secondary dengue fever with severe thrombocytopenia, mucocutaneous bleeding, acute hepatitis, and oropharyngeal candidiasis on a background of poorly controlled diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 10%), confirmed by positive dengue NS1 antigen ELISA. Managed with supportive care, random donor platelet transfusions, oral nystatin suspension (4 mL QID), and subcutaneous regular insulin (10 U TID), achieving complete resolution of throat pain and clinical recovery over 2 weeks.
